claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an fcc matrix in its as-built state.
Degradation in oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by selective oxidation or reduction of Al and Ti at grain boundaries and phase interfaces.
Selective oxidation or reduction at grain boundaries and phase interfaces causes embrittlement.
The proposed grain-boundary degradation can cause catastrophic intergranular failure.
Changing O2 or H2 partial pressure will reveal the governing degradation behavior through changes in grain-boundary chemistry and mechanical properties.
Al and Ti may segregate to grain boundaries and phase interfaces in the fcc matrix.
Oxidizing exposure forms Al- or Ti-containing brittle oxides at grain boundaries.
Reducing exposure can produce grain-boundary chemical changes or intermetallics involving Al and Ti.
Brittle oxides or intermetallics reduce grain-boundary cohesion and promote intergranular fracture.
Increasing O2 partial pressure will increase Al/Ti oxide formation at grain boundaries.
Increased grain-boundary Al/Ti oxide formation will produce greater embrittlement and lower fracture toughness.
Increasing H2 partial pressure may reduce or destabilize protective oxides.
Destabilization of protective oxides under H2 may lead to embrittlement.
Catastrophic failure occurs when grain-boundary degradation reaches a critical threshold.
The as-built baseline has minimal grain-boundary oxidation or embrittlement.
The hypothesis applies between 800 and 1000°C in atmospheres having significant O2 or H2 partial pressure.
The proposed mechanism does not apply at low temperatures or in inert atmospheres.
The hypothesis is falsified if grain-boundary chemical changes do not correlate with embrittlement or intergranular failure, or if degradation occurs without such chemical changes.
